newsitem.title: CANADA: Reform steals Liberal thunder in Canadian campaign.
newsitem.headline: Reform steals Liberal thunder in Canadian campaign.

text.p: The populist Reform Party has stolen the thunder of the ruling Liberals on the first week of Canada's election campaign, releasing the Liberals' platform ahead of schedule and putting its own anti-tax spin on it.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien's team scrambled to contain the damage by scheduling an emergency official release of the platform in the prairie city of Saskatoon later on Wednesday.
Chretien had planned to unveil the key campaign document for the June 2 federal election in Ottawa on Thursday.
He told reporters in Vancouver he was not sure who leaked it to Reform, adding: "If I knew there would be one employee less."

Chretien had used the platform, dubbed the Red Book, to great effect in sweeping to a solid majority in 1993. Red Book Two, the 1997 version, was supposed to give the Liberals new impetus as they near the end of a battle to eliminate fiscal deficits.

Waving a copy of the Red Book, which he said had been slipped to Reform Party headquarters, Reform leader Preston Manning told reporters on Tuesday in Quebec City: "It's goodbye Red Book, hello checkbook, and it is the Canadian taxpayer's checkbook we are talking about."
Reform released excerpts from Red Book Two and said the cost of new spending initiatives on which there was a price-tag would be C$6.5 billion (U.S. $4.6 billion) over the next five years.
In addition, the Liberals committed themselves to "pharmacare" -- national insurance for drugs -- "as a long-term national objective," Reform said.
Reform estimated, based on British Columbia's experience, that this could cost C$3.5 billion (U.S. $2.5 billion) a year.
"Is C$10 billion in possible new spending really consistent with fiscal restraint?" Reform asked in a statement commenting on the Liberals' spending plans.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) reported the new Red Book would commit the government to spending 50 percent of any budget surplus, allocating the other 50 percent to a combination of debt reduction and tax relief.
The Red Book, as quoted by Reform, said the time for a broad-based tax reduction would come "when we can afford it as a society and when Canadians can be assured that such cuts can be permanent."
But it also said: "To propose a broad-based tax reduction at this time is to pretend that the attack on the deficit is over, when it is not."
Chretien's government has slashed the budget deficit dramatically but is still counting on at least another two years to reach a balance.
Reform and the Conservative Party, both far behind the Liberals in the polls, are vying for the right-wing vote with promises to cut income and payroll taxes and to get tough on crime.

"This government had no money on Monday, now has billions of dollars on Tuesday, and it proves that they have no plan, certainly no sense of priorities," Conservative leader Jean Charest said in Ontario on Tuesday.
On the left, New Democratic Party (NDP) leader Alexa McDonough told a news conference that the Red Book was "The Retread Book."

A Compas poll published in Wednesday's Financial Post gave the Liberals 47 percent of decided voters against 18 percent to the Conservatives, 13 percent for Reform, 10 percent for the NDP and 11 percent for the separatist Bloc Quebecois.
The poll was taken from April 15 to 25, before Chretien's announcement of the election date.
